metadata.title: Linked Exponential Relations
metadata.description: Translate linked powers into substitution or small linear systems, then verify each result in the original relationships.
metadata.teachingApproach: Build rules from definitions, develop examples step by step, explain common misconceptions, and use exact checks. Each practice question has a targeted remedial explanation and a changed-value retry.
metadata.sourceScope: R.S. Aggarwal, Quantitative Aptitude for Competitive Examinations, Chapter 9 “Surds and Indices,” printed pages 278–288. Approved scope: Model linked relationships such as x=y^a, y=z^b, z=x^c by substitution and explain why a nonzero positive quantity allows the resulting power relation to be interpreted carefully. Teach systems of exponential equations by rewriting bases to a shared prime base, converting each equation into a linear relation among exponents, then solving the small simultaneous system. Include a consistency check in the original power equations and note special cases such as zero values or bases that make exponent comparison non-unique. Use only source-level algebra; do not invoke logarithms or assume variables are positive unless the problem or root definition establishes it.

content.text: Welcome to Linked Exponential Relations. We will build each rule from its meaning, work through exact examples, and use practice to check both the method and its conditions.

Some problems connect variables through powers, such as x=y^a, y=z^b, and z=x^c. The goal is to substitute one relationship into another until the same quantity is related to itself. Keep each substitution explicit so no exponent is lost.

For positive x,y,z, the chain x=y^a, y=z^b, z=x^c gives x=(x^c)^(b a)=x^(abc). If x>0 and x≠1, equality of powers with the same base yields abc=1. If x=1, the equation holds for any product abc, so that special case must not be ignored.

If a variable may be zero or negative, the chain needs more care because fractional powers may be undefined or non-unique over the reals. State the domain supplied by the problem and avoid applying exponent comparison outside it.

A second common pattern is a system of equations in exponents. Rewrite every numerical base as a power of the same prime, then equate exponents. For example, 8^x·2^y=512 becomes 2^(3x+y)=2^9, hence 3x+y=9.

A second equation can provide the other linear relation. Convert each independently, solve the resulting simultaneous equations using substitution or elimination, then substitute the values back into both exponent relations.

Example: 8^x·2^y=512 and 4^x·8^y=1024. The first becomes 3x+y=9; the second becomes 2x+3y=10. Eliminate y: multiply the first by 3 to get 9x+3y=27, subtract the second to get 7x=17, so x=17/7 and y=12/7. The unusual fractions are valid; verify the linear exponents are 9 and 10.

When every base is positive and not 1, matching the common prime-base powers is safe. If a rewritten equation has base 1, its exponent is not determined by its value. Check for this before concluding a unique pair.
A system may contain coefficients hidden in powers. Since 25^x=5^(2x), it contributes 2x, not x, to the exponent of 5. Make a conversion table: original base, prime base, exponent multiplier.

A useful table prevents mixing the two layers: the original exponential statement; its equivalent exponent equation; then the solved variable values. Do not write an exponent equation before the numerical bases have been aligned.

If the equations are dependent, they may fail to give a unique pair. For example, 2^x·4^y=64 and 8^x·16^y=4096 both reduce to the same equation x+2y=6. There are many pairs, so another independent condition would be needed.

Check an apparent solution by rebuilding each original side. If the values of x and y make the left exponent equal the target exponent in every equation, the common-base equivalence confirms the original powers agree.

A linked-power identity can also be checked with logarithms in advanced settings, but this topic stays within the source’s exponent laws and elementary equations. No logarithmic operation is needed or introduced here.

When a product relation yields x^k=x^m, do not cancel or divide by x unless x≠0. If x is nonzero and the powers are meaningful, one can often reduce the relation; if x=0 is allowed, test that case separately.

The common errors are swapping which exponent multiplies through a chain, assuming a unique solution from dependent equations, and matching exponents before converting to one base. Label each relationship before substituting.

In practice, first identify whether the problem is a substitution chain or a system. For a system, make a common-base equation for each line. For a chain, substitute in one direction and test any exceptional base values.
Give the requested variable, not merely the linear relation or an intermediate exponent. A final substitution into the original statements is the strongest quick check.

inlineData.explanation: The equations become x+3y=12 and 2x+y=10. From the second, x=(10−y)/2. Substitute: (10−y)/2+3y=12, so 10−y+6y=24, 5y=14, and y=14/5. Then x=18/5. Check both equations: 18/5+42/5=12 and 36/5+14/5=10.
